title: Major Surveys and Indices
breadcrumb: Official Statistics → Indian Statistical System → Major surveys and indices
engineName: Institutions and official statistics — what India measures, how often, and on what base
provenance: Re-audited on 14 November 2026 against current official sources. HCES definitions, periodicity, MPCE, food shares and the correctly labelled urban-rural gap were checked against the 2023-24 official factsheet; the 2017-18 non-publication reason against the 8 August 2022 Rajya Sabha answer. PLFS redesign and sample facts were checked against MoSPI's 2025 redesign note and PLFS 2025 annual report. CPI, IIP and WPI/PPI series and the five-year transition were checked against the official PIB press release of 2 June 2026 (Release ID 2267963); the OEA portal itself timed out but the primary PIB release was accessible. HCES is conducted at regular intervals, not on a guaranteed decennial cycle; 2022-23 and 2023-24 were back-to-back. It supplies CPI budget shares and consumption data for poverty analysis, but does not itself set official poverty estimates. The 2017-18 results were not published because of data-quality issues.
HCES 2023-24: MPCE about ₹4,122 rural and ₹6,996 urban; food share about 47% rural, 40% urban.
Urban-rural MPCE difference as % of rural MPCE: 69.7% in 2023-24, 71.2% in 2022-23 and 83.9% in 2011-12. This is not rural MPCE as a percentage of urban MPCE.
PLFS launched 2017, replacing the quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Survey.
PLFS reference periods: Usual Status (ps+ss) 365 days; Current Weekly Status 7 days.
PLFS from Jan 2025: monthly all-India CWS; quarterly rural + urban + combined; calendar annual year.
PLFS sample: 22,692 FSUs × 12 households ≈ 2.72 lakh, from 12,800 × 8 ≈ 1.02 lakh; four visits per household.

ASI = annual sample survey of registered factories plus specified additional units, including 100+ employee units listed in State BRE where shared; latest reference year 2024-25 (detailed release 4 Nov 2026). ASUSE = unincorporated non-agricultural establishments; latest ASUSE 2025 (detailed release 6 May 2026).
NFHS: MoHFW with IIPS Mumbai. Published rounds listed here through NFHS-5 (2019-21); do not quote NFHS-6 indicators without its official report.

CPI base 2024=100 from 12 Feb 2026; weights from HCES 2023-24; COICOP 2018; 358 items; 1,465 villages and 1,407 urban markets. Six-group comparison weights: food 40.10%, housing 11.88%; do not confuse with COICOP division weights.
CPI is a modified Laspeyres index: Jevons at the elementary level, Young/modified Laspeyres above it.
WPI base revised 2011-12 → 2022-23; 957 items; goods only; Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT.

Output PPI launched 15 June 2026; WPI base 2022-23 continues during a five-year transition and is intended to be discontinued after that period. Trial Input PPI and quarterly Services PPI also introduced.
IIP base 2022-23=100; first monthly release 1 June 2026, revised 29 June 2026 to use Output PPI as deflator; 1,042 products in 463 item groups; NIC 2025.
IIP sector weights: manufacturing 76.062, mining 11.053, electricity and gas 10.865, water and sewerage 2.020.
IIP use-based: primary 31.136, intermediate 22.416, consumer non-durables 16.147, durables 11.311, infra 10.908, capital 8.082.
CPI linking factors 0.5222 / 0.5320 / 0.5267 — new over old, so MULTIPLY the old index.

IIP linking factors: general 1.3834; mining 1.1890; manufacturing 1.3700; electricity 1.8495. Defined old-over-new, so divide old-series values. Water-supply sector is new and has no direct old-series factor.

tricks.hook: Calendar for consumers, financial for the rest
tricks.why: CPI moved to calendar 2024; IIP and WPI both moved to financial 2022-23. One word separates the three.

tricks.hook: Only one index is being killed
tricks.why: CPI and IIP were rebased. WPI and PPI series are published concurrently; distinguish publication from GDP deflator use.

tricks.hook: MoSPI does CPI and IIP; DPIIT does WPI and PPI
tricks.why: The producer is asked as often as the base year, and the two price indices sit in different ministries.

tricks.hook: Surveys measure quantities, indices reprice them
tricks.why: It is the whole architecture in six words, and it tells you which body produces which number.

CPI factors are published for the general index and use new-over-old (multiply); IIP factors are available for the general index and major sectors and use old-over-new (divide); WPI publishes factors for All Commodities and major groups.

shortcuts: Any option giving CPI a financial-year base is wrong; any option giving IIP or WPI a calendar base is wrong.
Any option that has WPI covering services is wrong — that is the Services PPI.
Any option naming MoSPI as the producer of WPI is wrong, and vice versa for CPI.
If a question names the previous consumption round before 2022-23, the answer is 2011-12, never 2017-18.
Gas supply is inside the electricity sector of the IIP; the genuinely new sector is water and sewerage.
remember: Locate any unfamiliar fact on the chain: survey → weights → index → deflator → national accounts.
Before applying a linking factor, read whether it is defined as new over old or old over new.
traps: Assuming WPI publication ended when PPI was introduced; WPI continues during a five-year transition and is intended to be discontinued after it.
Giving the CPI a 2022-23 base because the other two indices have it.
Treating WPI and PPI as permanently parallel; the current arrangement is a five-year transition.
Calling gas supply a new IIP sector; it is inside electricity, and water supply is the new sector.

Quoting the COICOP division food weight (36.75%) as the group-table weight (40.10%), or the reverse.
Multiplying by the IIP linking factor and dividing by the CPI one, which is the wrong way round for both.

WPI covers goods only and is produced by DPIIT, not MoSPI.
WPI and PPI series are published concurrently; do not infer WPI discontinuation from PPI availability.
The consumption round before 2022-23 is 2011-12; the 2017-18 round was withheld.
Water supply and sewerage is the new IIP sector; gas supply sits inside electricity.
The CPI linking factor is new over old, so it multiplies; the IIP factor is defined the other way round.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Have the index-number machinery and the survey vocabulary ready, so the institutional facts attach to ideas rather than floating free.
body: This topic sits at the join of two things you already half-know. One is index numbers, which you met as formulae. The other is sample surveys, which you met as designs. Unit X asks what India actually builds with them, and the questions are a mark each.

The four checks below are the machinery. If they are solid, the rest of this lesson is a set of names, years and weights hung on a frame you already have. If they are not, the names will be a list to forget.

items.ask: Write the Laspeyres, Paasche and Fisher price index formulae, and say which weights each uses.
items.recall: Laspeyres uses base-period quantities: P_L = Σp₁q₀ / Σp₀q₀. Paasche uses current-period quantities: P_P = Σp₁q₁ / Σp₀q₁. Fisher is their geometric mean: P_F = √(P_L × P_P).
refresh: The whole difference is which basket you price. Laspeyres asks what the base-year basket costs now; Paasche asks what the current basket would have cost then. Laspeyres needs quantities only once, so it is what statistical offices actually use.

Laspeyres has an upward bias and Paasche a downward one, because neither lets the basket respond to the price change it is measuring. Fisher's geometric mean splits the difference and satisfies the time-reversal and factor-reversal tests, which is why it is called the ideal index.
India's CPI is a modified Laspeyres index — a fixed basket, repriced. That one sentence explains why the basket has to be replaced every so often, which is what a base-year revision is.

items.ask: What is a base year, and what does it mean to rebase an index and link the two series?
items.recall: The base year is the period set equal to 100, whose basket and weights the index carries. Rebasing replaces that period, basket and weight set. Linking is the arithmetic that puts the old series onto the new base, using a factor estimated from a period in which both series ran.
refresh: An index with a fixed basket drifts out of date: items disappear, new ones appear, and spending patterns move. Rebasing resets the basket to a recent consumption or production pattern.

The cost is comparability. The new series is not the old one continued, so a linking factor is computed from an overlap period and applied to the old numbers. It works at the top level and usually nowhere below it, because the two baskets are not classified the same way.

Keep a sharp distinction between a base year being revised and a series being discontinued. Both have happened in India recently, to different indices, and a question will put one where the other belongs.

items.ask: What is a multistage stratified sample, and what is a first stage unit?
items.recall: A design that selects larger units first and smaller ones within them, with the population divided into strata and sampling done independently inside each. The first stage unit is the larger unit selected first — in Indian household surveys, a census village in rural areas and an urban frame survey block in towns.
refresh: You cannot list every household in India, so you list villages and blocks, select some, then list households only inside the selected ones. That is the multistage idea, and it exists to make the frame manageable.

Stratification — by state, by district, by distance from a city — reduces variance and guarantees that each stratum is represented. Sampling independently within strata is what lets the office publish state-level numbers.

The arithmetic to carry: sample size in these surveys is usually quoted as first stage units times households per unit. When a survey is redesigned, those two numbers are what change, and the exam asks for them.

items.ask: What is the difference between a nominal and a real series, and what is a deflator?
items.recall: A nominal series is measured in the prices of its own period; a real series is measured in the prices of a fixed period, so that only quantity changes remain. A deflator is the price index used to divide the nominal series into the real one.
refresh: If output in rupees rose 12% and prices rose 5%, real output rose by roughly 7% — more precisely, by the ratio of the two indices. The price index doing the dividing is the deflator.

This is where the indices in this lesson stop being bookkeeping. The wholesale index is the deflator for much of the industrial production series; the consumer index is the one that enters wage indexation and the inflation target.
So a change in one index propagates. That is the reason base-year revisions are news, and the reason the exam treats the three indices as one connected system rather than three separate facts.

scenes.title: Why surveys and indices are one topic
scenes.objective: See the chain that runs from a household interview to the inflation number, so the facts have an order.
body: A syllabus line that reads 'major surveys and indices' looks like two lists to memorise. It is really one chain, and the chain is what makes the facts stick.

Start at the bottom. A household survey asks what people bought and what it cost. Aggregate that and you have a consumption pattern — the share of spending that goes on cereals, rent, transport, phone bills. That pattern is the weight set for a price index. The price index is then produced monthly from a far cheaper operation: field staff who only collect prices, not quantities, because the quantities are frozen in the weights.

HCES is conducted at regular intervals, not on a guaranteed decennial cycle. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 rounds were deliberately run back to back to support revision of macroeconomic base years. The 2023-24 survey supplied the consumption budget shares used for the CPI 2024=100 weighting diagram.

The same logic runs on the production side. The Annual Survey of Industries is an annual sample survey of selected eligible factories and other industrial establishments, not a census of every factory. It describes the industrial sector and supports analysis of its structure; monthly production indices then track a fixed basket of items with weights. National accounts use several price indices as deflators, but not every deflator is a CPI or WPI.
That is the whole architecture: surveys set the weights, indices run on them, accounts consume both.

aside.h: The sentence to carry into the exam
aside.body: Surveys are infrequent and measure quantities; indices are frequent and measure prices against frozen quantities. A base-year revision is the moment the newest survey replaces the old weights.

ask.q: If the consumer price index freezes quantities from a survey, what happens to measured inflation when people respond to a price rise by buying less of the item?
ask.nudge: Think about which basket is being priced, and whether the index is allowed to notice the substitution.

scenes.title: The National Sample Survey and what grew out of it
scenes.objective: Place the NSS, its round structure, and the four surveys that now descend from it.

blocks.h: The National Sample Survey
blocks.body: Set up in 1950 on Mahalanobis's design, the National Sample Survey is the country's large-scale household survey programme and one of the oldest in the world. Work is organised into rounds, each round covering a set of subjects over a stated period. Rounds that carry a full-scale subject enquiry are the large or quinquennial rounds; the lighter ones in between are the thin rounds. The field and processing organisation, the NSSO, was merged into the National Statistical Office in 2019, so current releases say NSO, MoSPI.

blocks.h: What the programme covers
blocks.body: Household consumption expenditure; employment and unemployment; land and livestock holdings; debt and investment; housing conditions; health, education and social consumption; unincorporated enterprises; and the Annual Survey of Industries on the factory side. The subjects rotate across rounds, which is why a question about 'which round covered X' is a question about the rotation.

blocks.h: The four you must be able to name
blocks.body: HCES — Household Consumption Expenditure Survey, the consumption survey. It collects household consumption and expenditure and supplies budget shares used to prepare CPI weights; it also provides data used in poverty analysis, but it does not itself set the official poverty line or issue official poverty estimates. PLFS — Periodic Labour Force Survey, the labour survey, which replaced the quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Survey in 2017. ASI — Annual Survey of Industries, covering registered factories and specified additional industrial establishments. ASUSE — Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises, covering unincorporated non-agricultural establishments; it is not simply the 'unregistered counterpart' of ASI.

blocks.h: ASI and ASUSE — the two halves of one picture
blocks.body: ASI broadly covers factories registered under sections 2m(i) and 2m(ii) of the Factories Act, 1948; bidi and cigar manufacturing establishments registered under the 1966 Act; electricity undertakings not registered with the CEA; and units with 100 or more employees registered in State Business Registers where the State shares the list. Data are collected from selected establishments under the Collection of Statistics Act, 2008 as amended in 2017, through a dedicated web portal. The latest published results are for the 2024-25 reference year (April 2024–March 2025): the factsheet was released on 30 September 2026 and the detailed Volume I and Summary Results on 4 November 2026. ASUSE covers unincorporated establishments in manufacturing, trade and services, excluding construction; its latest annual results are ASUSE 2025 (January–December 2025), with the factsheet released 24 March 2026 and detailed report 6 May 2026.

blocks.h: Surveys outside MoSPI
blocks.body: Two major surveys belong to other ministries and are examined all the same. The National Family Health Survey is run by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with the International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai, as nodal agency; NFHS-5 covers 2019-21, and NFHS-6 outcome figures should not be quoted without the corresponding official report. The Annual Health Survey was a separate historical sample survey, while the Sample Registration System is an ongoing demographic sample system. Neither is the Civil Registration System (CRS): the CRS is the legal administrative registration system for births and deaths.

blocks.h: The 2017-18 round that was never published
blocks.body: A consumption round was fielded in 2017-18, but MoSPI did not publish the results because of data-quality issues identified during its vetting. The Ministry's Rajya Sabha reply of 8 August 2022 describes the significant variation found in the results and explains that 2011-12 remained the latest published HCES round until 2022-23. Do not attribute non-publication to the leak of figures unless a primary source is cited. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 rounds are not directly comparable with 2011-12 because methodology and reference-period details changed.

blocks.h: The NFHS rounds, since they are asked plainly
blocks.body: NFHS-1 1992-93, NFHS-2 1998-99, NFHS-3 2005-06, NFHS-4 2015-16, NFHS-5 2019-21. Quote round-specific indicators with the correct reference period; avoid assuming NFHS-6 results are released.

scenario.teaser: A completed national survey whose results were never published — and the eleven-year hole it left.
scenario.title: The consumption round of 2017-18
body: A consumption survey was fielded across India in 2017-18. The field work was done, the data were processed, and a report was prepared. In November 2019 the government announced that the results would not be released, citing the quality of the data. By then figures from the draft had already appeared in the press.

The decision is the reason the published consumption series runs 2011-12, then nothing, then 2022-23. The gap matters because HCES provides the household consumption data used in CPI weighting and poverty analysis. It does not itself set the official poverty line; the Government's poverty-estimation methodology has been determined through expert groups and the responsible planning authority.

The episode belongs in this topic for three reasons. It explains the gap, which is a factual question. It explains why two consumption rounds were run back to back in 2022-23 and 2023-24 to rebuild a current consumption series; HCES has been conducted at regular intervals, not on a guaranteed single quinquennial or decennial schedule. And it is a concrete case behind the wider concern about the credibility and quality assurance of official statistics.

Treat the facts carefully in an answer. What is established is that the round was conducted, that the results were withheld in November 2019, and that the stated reason was data quality. Whether the data were in fact poor is contested, and an exam answer does not need to take a side on it.
scenario.close: A survey is only as useful as its publication: the 2017-18 round was completed and is still, statistically speaking, missing.

scenes.title: HCES and PLFS — the two surveys that changed recently
scenes.objective: State what each survey measures, the figures it produced, and exactly what the 2025 redesign changed.

blocks.h: HCES — what it measures
blocks.body: Monthly per capita consumption expenditure, MPCE, item by item, separately for rural and urban areas and by expenditure class. Two consecutive rounds were run after the long gap: 2022-23 and 2023-24. The 2023-24 round put average MPCE at about ₹4,122 rural and ₹6,996 urban, or ₹4,247 and ₹7,078 once the imputed value of free benefits is added.

blocks.h: The two HCES numbers that get asked
blocks.body: Food share of consumption in 2023-24 was 47.04% rural and 39.68% urban. It rose slightly from 2022-23 (46.38% rural and 39.17% urban), but remained below 2011-12 levels (52.90% rural and 42.62% urban). The urban-rural gap in MPCE, expressed as a percentage of rural MPCE, was 83.9% in 2011-12, 71.2% in 2022-23 and 69.7% in 2023-24. Do not call 69.7% the rural MPCE as a percentage of urban MPCE: it is (urban MPCE − rural MPCE) / rural MPCE × 100. The published measure shows a narrowing relative gap.

blocks.h: PLFS — what it measures
blocks.body: Labour Force Participation Rate, Worker Population Ratio and Unemployment Rate, under two reference periods. Usual Status (principal plus subsidiary) classifies a person by activity over the preceding 365 days; Current Weekly Status classifies by the preceding 7 days. PLFS was launched in 2017 and replaced the quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Survey, which had produced an estimate only every five years.

blocks.h: What PLFS looked like before 2025
blocks.body: Quarterly estimates for urban areas only, on Current Weekly Status. Annual estimates for rural and urban, on both Usual Status and CWS, for a July-to-June year. About 12,800 first stage units a year, 8 households each, roughly 1,02,400 households.

blocks.h: What the January 2025 redesign changed
blocks.body: Four things. First, monthly all-India estimates of LFPR, WPR and UR on CWS for rural and urban, which did not exist before; the first monthly bulletin was for April 2025. Second, quarterly estimates extended from urban only to rural, urban and combined, including major states. Third, the annual year moved from July-June to the calendar year, from 2025. Fourth, the sample: 22,692 first stage units a year and 12 households each, about 2,72,304 households — roughly 2.65 times the old size.

blocks.h: And the design behind it
blocks.body: A multistage stratified design in which the basic stratum is now the district for most areas rather than the NSS region, with rural areas further stratified by distance from the district headquarters or from a city of over five lakh, and urban areas by million-plus cities. Each selected household is visited four times in consecutive months — one first visit and three revisits — which is the rotational panel that makes monthly estimates possible.

blocks.h: The comparability warning
blocks.body: MoSPI's own note says estimates from January 2025 onwards should not be compared casually with those published up to December 2024. A question that asks you to read a trend across that boundary is testing whether you know the break is there.

scenes.objective: Retrieve the survey facts before the three indices are added, so the two halves stay separate.
scenes.intro: Answer aloud, then look. Everything here was in the last two scenes.

items.q: Which survey supplies the weights for the consumer price index, and which round did it for the 2024 base?
items.a: The Household Consumption Expenditure Survey — the 2023-24 round.

items.q: What did PLFS replace, and in what year was PLFS launched?
items.a: The quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Survey; PLFS was launched in 2017.

items.q: Give the two PLFS reference periods and their windows.
items.a: Usual Status (principal plus subsidiary), 365 days; Current Weekly Status, 7 days.

items.q: Which two surveys cover the registered and the unregistered non-agricultural sectors?
items.a: ASI covers registered factories; ASUSE covers unincorporated enterprises.

items.q: Why does the consumption series skip from 2011-12 to 2022-23?
items.a: The 2017-18 round's results were withheld in November 2019 on grounds of data quality.

items.q: Who runs the National Family Health Survey, and through which nodal agency?
items.a: The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, through the International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai.

scenes.problem: Fill in each blank with the figure or name the lesson has given.

steps.say: The consumer price index was rebased, from one base year to another.

blank.prompt: From which base to which base?
blank.hint: The new base is a calendar year in which base prices were collected.

steps.why: Every other fact about the new series hangs on knowing which two bases are involved.

steps.say: The item basket and weights of that new series came from a survey.

blank.hint: The consumption survey, in its second post-gap round.

steps.why: This is the link between the two halves of the topic, and the most asked single fact in it.

steps.say: The index of industrial production was also rebased.

blank.hint: A financial year, not a calendar year — and the same one the wholesale index moved to.

steps.why: The CPI base is a calendar year and the IIP base a financial year; the pairing is examinable.

steps.say: The WPI and PPI are now published in parallel.

blank.answer: Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT
blank.hint: The output version of it launched alongside the revised wholesale index.

steps.why: PPI is used for selected GDP deflation purposes, but that does not mean WPI publication has ended.

steps.say: PLFS now publishes an estimate at a frequency it did not before 2025.

blank.prompt: Which frequency, on which reference period?
accept: monthly estimates using current weekly status
blank.hint: The seven-day reference period, not the 365-day one.

steps.why: Monthly on CWS is the headline change of 2025 and the one most likely to appear as a single-mark question.

scenes.after: Two base years, one survey, one replacement index and one new frequency. Those five facts carry most of the marks this topic offers.

scenes.title: The three indices, and where they now stand
scenes.objective: State each index's base year, weights, producer and current status, and keep the three apart.

blocks.h: CPI — Consumer Price Index, base 2024=100
blocks.body: Produced by the NSO, MoSPI. The first release on the new base was on 12 February 2026, replacing base 2012=100. The basket and weights come from HCES 2023-24; base-period prices were collected through calendar 2024. Rural, urban and combined indices are published, the combined being a weighted average of the other two. It is a modified Laspeyres index: elementary indices use the Jevons formula, higher-level indices a Young or modified Laspeyres formula.

blocks.h: What changed in the CPI basket
blocks.body: Classification moved to COICOP 2018 — twelve divisions in place of six groups, resolving to 43 groups, 92 classes, 162 subclasses and 358 items, up from 299. Goods rose from 259 to 308 and services from 40 to 50. In the six-group comparison table, food and beverages carry 40.10% against 45.86% before, and housing 11.88% against 10.07%; these are legacy group-comparison weights, not the COICOP division weights. Rural house rent entered the index for the first time. Prices are collected from 1,465 villages and 1,407 urban markets (including online markets), using handheld devices; e-commerce prices are collected in twelve large towns and administrative data are used for selected items such as rail fares, postal charges and fuel.

blocks.h: WPI and the parallel PPI series
blocks.body: The wholesale price index measures prices of goods only — no services — at the wholesale or first point of bulk sale, and is produced by the Office of the Economic Adviser in DPIIT, not by MoSPI. Its base was revised from 2011-12 to 2022-23 and the basket expanded from 697 to 957 items. On 15 June 2026, the Output Producer Price Index (OPPI), a trial Input PPI for manufacturing, and a quarterly Services PPI covering seven sectors were introduced. WPI continues during a five-year transition from the PPI launch and is intended to be discontinued after that period; do not describe it as having stopped on 15 June 2026.

blocks.h: IIP — Index of Industrial Production, base 2022-23=100
blocks.body: Produced by the NSO. The Technical Advisory Committee report for the new series was released on 25 May 2026; the first monthly release on base 2022-23 came on 1 June 2026, replacing base 2011-12. The basket holds 1,042 products mapped to 463 item groups, against 839 and 407 before, and uses NIC 2025. Important release-history trap: the 1 June series used WPI as the deflator, but MoSPI's 29 June 2026 release superseded it with a revised series using Output PPI as the deflator. For current analysis, use the revised PPI-based series, not the initial June 1 release.

blocks.h: IIP weights, both ways of cutting them
blocks.body: By sector: manufacturing 76.062, mining and quarrying 11.053, electricity and gas supply 10.865, and — new to the index — water supply, sewerage and waste management 2.020. Gas supply is inside the electricity sector with a weight of 0.694, not a sector of its own. By use: primary goods 31.136, intermediate goods 22.416, consumer non-durables 16.147, consumer durables 11.311, infrastructure and construction goods 10.908, capital goods 8.082. The movement worth remembering is intermediate goods up from 17.221 and mining down from 14.372.

blocks.h: Who produces what
blocks.body: MoSPI through the NSO: CPI, IIP, national accounts and NSS surveys. DPIIT through the Office of the Economic Adviser: WPI and PPI. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare through IIPS: NFHS. The RBI's monetary-policy target is headline CPI inflation measured using CPI-Combined; the notified target for 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031 remains 4 per cent with a 2–6 per cent tolerance band. RBI uses the index but does not produce it.

blocks.h: Three indices, three different revisions
blocks.body: CPI moved to a calendar base year, 2024. IIP and WPI both moved to a financial year, 2022-23. WPI and the new producer-price indices are published during the five-year transition; WPI is intended to be discontinued after the transition. IIP's first 1 June 2026 release was WPI-deflated, but the 29 June 2026 release superseded it with the revised Output-PPI-deflated series. Distinguish index publication from use of a price index as a GDP deflator.

scenario.teaser: Rural rent had never been in the Indian consumer price index. In 2026 it was, and the housing weight moved.
scenario.title: How a survey becomes a basket
body: Follow one item through the machinery. Under the old CPI, base 2012=100, the housing index covered urban house rent only. Rural housing was outside the index altogether, on the reasoning that most rural households own their dwellings and pay no rent, so there was nothing to price.

The 2023-24 consumption survey measured what rural households actually spend on housing — rent where it is paid, and the maintenance, repair, water supply and related services that every household pays whether it owns or rents. That spending turned out to be large enough to belong in the index.

So the new series, base 2024=100, does three things at once with housing. It includes rural house rent for the first time. It redefines the housing index as a weighted average of actual rent, maintenance and repair, and water supply and miscellaneous services. And the housing weight rises from 10.07% to 11.88%, which is not a judgement by the statistical office but an arithmetic consequence of what the survey found.

The same survey did the same work for every other item. Streaming services came in, having not existed in a meaningful way in 2012. Out went VCR and DVD players, radios, tape recorders, second-hand clothing, CDs and DVDs, and coir rope. Food and beverages fell from 45.86% to 40.10% in the group table — not because food got cheaper, but because households now spend a smaller share of a larger budget on it.
That last sentence is the one examiners like. A falling weight is a statement about budget shares, not about prices or about hardship, and reading it as the latter is a standard error.
scenario.close: A weight is a measured consumption share, not a policy choice: the survey decides it, and the index inherits it.

scenes.title: Linking two series — the arithmetic
scenes.objective: Convert a figure from an old base to a new one, and know why the direction cannot be memorised.

blocks.h: What a linking factor is for
blocks.body: A linking factor lets an old series be expressed on a new base, but its definition and availability differ by index. CPI's published linking factors are at the general-index level; its old and new sub-group classifications do not support a reliable direct sub-index link. IIP provides factors for the general index and major sectors. The WPI 2022-23 release provides linking factors for All Commodities and major groups. Always use the factor and direction specified in the relevant official release.

blocks.h: The CPI case, which is the one to carry
blocks.body: MoSPI defines the CPI linking factor as the annual geometric mean of the new series in 2025 divided by that of the old series in 2025 — the overlap year in which both were published. The factors are 0.5222 rural, 0.5320 urban and 0.5267 combined. Because the factor is new over old, you MULTIPLY an old-base figure by it: an old combined index of 200 becomes 200 × 0.5267 = 105.34 on base 2024=100.

blocks.h: And why the IIP case runs the other way
blocks.body: For the IIP 2022-23 series, the general linking factor is 1.3834; the published sector factors are 1.1890 for mining, 1.3700 for manufacturing and 1.8495 for electricity. The new water-supply, sewerage and waste-management sector has no direct old-series counterpart. The factor is defined as the geometric mean of the OLD series during the new base year divided by that of the new series in the same year. With that definition, an old-base figure is DIVIDED by the factor to reach the new base. Read the definition before applying it.

blocks.h: What this means for growth rates
blocks.body: A linked series is a convenience, not a continuation. MoSPI says explicitly that growth rates across the two IIP series are not strictly comparable, because coverage, basket, sectoral composition and weights changed. CPI sub-indices also cannot be directly linked where the old and new classifications do not align. An exam statement claiming that every linked series is fully comparable is false.

blocks.h: One number worth a sanity check
blocks.body: The January 2026 CPI combined provisional index on base 2024=100 was 104.46, with year-on-year inflation of 2.75%. Divide 104.46 by 0.5267 and you get about 198.3, which is where the old series stood. If a question gives you one of these and asks for the other, that is the whole calculation.

scenes.title: Work through a linking and a weight calculation
scenes.objective: Do the two pieces of arithmetic this topic actually asks for.
scenes.problem: (a) The CPI combined index on base 2012=100 stood at 189.4 in a given month. What is the equivalent figure on base 2024=100? (b) In the new IIP series, manufacturing carries 76.062 and electricity and gas supply 10.865, of which gas supply is 0.694. What weight does electricity alone carry, and by how many points did the combined electricity-and-gas weight rise over the 2011-12 series, where electricity alone carried 7.995?
hints: For (a), decide first whether the CPI factor is new-over-old or old-over-new, then multiply or divide accordingly.
For (b), the sector weight is the sum of its parts; subtract to isolate electricity.
For the rise in (b), compare like with like: the old series had no gas inside the sector, so compare the old electricity-only weight with the new sector total, and say so.

solution.say: (a) The CPI linking factor is defined as the new series mean over the old series mean in the overlap year 2025, so it converts old to new by multiplication. The combined factor is 0.5267.
Multiply the old-base figure by it.
A sanity check: the answer is just under 100, and 100 is the 2024 average. An old-base figure of 189.4 therefore sits a shade below the new base period, which is consistent.
solution.math: 99.76 < 100 → the month is a little below the 2024 average

solution.say: (b) The sector total is electricity plus gas, so electricity alone is the remainder.

For the rise, the honest comparison states what moved. Electricity alone went from 7.995 to 10.171, a rise of 2.176 points; the sector as now defined carries 10.865, which is 2.870 points above the old electricity-only weight.

scenes.answer: (a) 99.76 on base 2024=100. (b) Electricity alone 10.171; a like-for-like rise of 2.176 points, or 2.870 points if the redefined sector total is compared with the old electricity-only weight.
scenes.check: If (a) came out near 360, you divided instead of multiplying. Check the direction against the base period: a figure on base 2024=100 for a month near 2024 has to be near 100, and 360 is not.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Meet the exact confusions the paper builds between the three indices and the surveys.
scenes.intro: Each is either the standard fact or one detail moved from a neighbouring index.

items.claim: The consumer price index on base 2024=100 takes its weights from the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023-24.
items.why: And base-period prices were collected through calendar 2024. The first release on the new base was in February 2026.

items.claim: The wholesale price index covers both goods and services.
items.why: WPI is a goods-only index. Services are covered by the new quarterly Services PPI, across seven sectors, which is one of the reasons for moving to a producer price framework at all.

items.claim: The index of industrial production and the wholesale price index were both rebased to 2022-23.
items.why: Both moved to the financial year 2022-23. Only CPI moved to a calendar base year, 2024. This is the pairing to hold: two financial years and one calendar year.

items.claim: PLFS was launched in 2017 and replaced the quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Survey.
items.why: Its original design gave quarterly urban estimates on Current Weekly Status and annual rural-and-urban estimates on both reference periods. The 2025 redesign added monthly all-India estimates.

items.claim: Gas supply is a separate sector in the new IIP series, alongside mining, manufacturing and electricity.
items.why: Gas supply sits inside Electricity and Gas Supply, with a weight of 0.694 within the sector's 10.865. What is genuinely new as a sector is water supply, sewerage and waste management, at 2.020.

items.claim: The consumption survey immediately preceding the 2022-23 round was the round of 2017-18.
items.why: A round was fielded in 2017-18 but its results were withheld in November 2019, so the last published round before 2022-23 is 2011-12. The series has a gap, not a continuous sequence.

scenes.title: Transfer — a case the lesson has not shown you
scenes.objective: Reason from the architecture when the question asks about something you were never given directly.
scenes.problem: A question asks: 'The Reserve Bank's inflation target is specified in terms of which index, and why is that index rather than the wholesale index used for the purpose?' Neither the target nor the reason appears in your notes as a fact to memorise. How do you answer, and how confident should you be?
hints: Ask which index measures what households actually pay, and which measures what wholesalers charge.
Ask which of the two covers services, and whether a target that ignores services could work.
Consider which index is published rural, urban and combined, and what a national target needs.

solution.say: The target has to be about the cost of living, because that is what monetary policy is accountable for. Between the two, CPI measures retail prices paid by households; WPI measures bulk prices charged earlier in the chain.
solution.math: Target = household cost of living → CPI, not WPI

solution.say: Second, WPI excludes services entirely, and services are a large and growing share of household spending — 50 of the 358 items in the new CPI basket are services. A goods-only index cannot stand in for the cost of living.
solution.math: WPI = goods only; CPI services = 50 items

solution.say: Third, CPI is published rural, urban and combined, and the combined index is the one a national target needs. So the answer is CPI-Combined, and the confidence is high, because three independent features of the two indices all point the same way.

scenes.answer: CPI-Combined, because the target concerns retail prices faced by households, because WPI covers no services, and because CPI alone is published as a rural-urban combined national index.
scenes.check: The method generalises: when a question asks which index is used for a purpose, ask what the purpose measures, then which index's coverage and publication level match it. You rarely need to have memorised the answer.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Compress the topic to the facts and the one habit the exam rewards.
body: Surveys. NSS from 1950, with large and thin rounds used at different times. NSSO was merged into the National Statistical Office in 2019. HCES measures MPCE and supplies CPI budget shares; it provides consumption data used in poverty analysis but does not itself set official poverty estimates. HCES rounds 2022-23 and 2023-24: average MPCE about ₹4,122 rural and ₹6,996 urban, food shares 47.04% and 39.68%, and the urban-rural MPCE gap (urban minus rural, as a percentage of rural MPCE) at 69.7%, down from 83.9% in 2011-12. Do not misstate this as rural MPCE being 69.7% of urban MPCE. The 2017-18 round was not published due to data-quality issues identified by MoSPI.

PLFS, launched 2017, replaced the quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Survey; Usual Status is 365 days and Current Weekly Status 7 days. From January 2025: monthly all-India CWS estimates, quarterly extended to rural and combined, a calendar annual year, and 22,692 first stage units with 12 households each — about 2.72 lakh households against about 1.02 lakh.

ASI is an annual sample survey, not a census. It covers Factories Act-registered factories plus specified additional establishments, including units with 100 or more employees listed in State Business Registers when shared. Latest ASI results: reference year 2024-25, detailed report released 4 November 2026. ASUSE covers unincorporated non-agricultural establishments in manufacturing, trade and services excluding construction; ASUSE 2025 is the latest annual release (factsheet 24 March, detailed report 6 May 2026). NFHS is run by MoHFW with IIPS Mumbai; do not quote unverified NFHS-6 outcome statistics.

Indices. CPI base 2024=100, first release February 2026, weights from HCES 2023-24, COICOP 2018, 358 items and 1,407 urban markets plus 1,465 villages; the six-group comparison weights (food 40.10%, housing 11.88%) must not be confused with COICOP division weights. WPI base 2022-23, 957 goods, produced by OEA/DPIIT; Output PPI, trial Input PPI and quarterly Services PPI were introduced in June 2026, with WPI scheduled to continue for five years before discontinuation. IIP base 2022-23, 1,042 products in 463 item groups on NIC 2025; its initial 1 June WPI-deflated release was superseded on 29 June by the current Output-PPI-deflated series.

Linking. CPI factors are published at the general-index level and use new-over-old, so multiply: 0.5267 combined. IIP factors are available for the general index and major sectors; the general factor 1.3834 and sector factors are old-over-new, so divide. WPI linking factors are available for All Commodities and major groups. Linked growth rates remain subject to comparability caveats.

The habit. Every fact in this topic belongs to a chain — survey sets weights, index runs on them, accounts use the index as a deflator. When a question gives you something you have not memorised, locate it on that chain and the answer usually follows.
